newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya publishes draft law to curb graft.
newsitem.headline: Kenya publishes draft law to curb graft.

text.p: The Kenyan Attorney-General published on Friday a tough anti-corruption bill to be debated and approved by parliament after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted an aid package in a row over graft.

Under "The Statute Law (Repeals and Miscellaneous Act) Bill 1997", Amos Wako also proposed to repeal the Vagrancy Act under which police can detain anyone on suspicion of being a vagabond and to amend various laws ranging from banking to public security.

The IMF decision to allow a key aid package to lapse over corruption hit Kenya earlier on Friday and forced the government to tighten belts to cover some of the immediate loss amid fears of much greater longer-term damage to the economy.
Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said the government had expected $215 million from the IMF and other donors in this financial year before the IMF halted crucial aid on Thursday.
"The government will concurrently cut its expenditure for this year and take revenue measures sufficient to address the shortfall of $141 million in external funding," he said.

Wako's bill appeared to fall far short of demands by an opposition-backed alliance pressing for political reforms as it proposed amendments in laws that deal with detention, public gatherings, registration of societies and parties rather than a total repeal.
The proposed changes also did not mention the electoral commission, which the opposition says is partisan. It also made no suggestions for making the state media more impartial.
Wako suggested tough measures to better regulate banking and in his anti-corruption bill, gave its head security of tenure, so the holder of office cannot be sacked on political grounds.

The anti-graft bill provides for an Authority to investigate corruption in government, determine liability and charge offenders in courts of law. It would become the first agency outside the attorney-general's office to receive such power.

"It is further proposed to amend the Public Order Act in order to replace the licencse requirement for the holding of public meetings and processions under existing law with a simple notification procedure," Wako's bill said.
But he also gave police powers to stop such gatherings.
In order to speed prosecutions in Kenyan courts, Wako proposed to increase the number of high court judges to 50 from 30 and court of appeal judges to 11 from eight.

On repealing the Vagrancy Act, Wako's said: "These laws are outdated and serve no useful purpose in the modern society of Kenya. Their repeal will enhance the enjoyment of human rights by all in Kenya."
An opposition-backed alliance campaigning for political reforms has called for a nationwide general strike on August 8 to put more pressure on Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years.

Foreign investors and tourists were already rattled by clashes between riot police and pro-reform demonstrators in June and July which culminated on July 7 with the deaths of at least nine people in Kenya's worst political unrest in seven years.
